articles.title: A Tennessee woman inherited her brother's house, then found strangers living there after a fake heir sold it while she was abroad; a court has revived her fraud claim against the title company, but not negligence
articles.summary: A Tennessee appeals court has revived the fraud claim of a woman who discovered, after returning to the United States from abroad in 2021, that the house
articles.body: A Tennessee appeals court has revived the fraud claim of a woman who discovered, after returning to the United States from abroad in 2021, that the house she had inherited from her late brother had been sold without her knowledge using a fake identity and forged documents. A woman using a fake identity had claimed to be the rightful heir. In its Thursday ruling, the court allowed Barbara Chesnut to pursue her fraud claim against the company involved in the sale but upheld the dismissal of her negligence claim.According to court records, Chesnut had acquired the house in Cottontown, Tennessee, in 2012 after her brother, James Upchurch, died without leaving a will. His estate was divided among several heirs, and Chesnut arranged to buy the property using her inheritance along with additional funds. She lived in the house before moving to the United Arab Emirates around the time the estate proceedings were being completed.While she moved overseas, Chesnut continued to use the Tennessee property as her permanent address and stayed there whenever she visited the United States. Between 2013 and 2014, she also allowed two people to live in the house. One of them was Vickie Podczervinski. Both occupants left sometime between 2016 and 2017, after which Chesnut returned and stayed for several months.She eventually went back to the UAE. When the Covid-19 pandemic disrupted international travel, she was unable to return to the United States for a considerable period. By the time she visited again in 2021, the house was occupied by people she did not recognise.Fake documents used to sell the houseThe sale had taken place in January 2020, when Chesnut was still overseas. Someone had presented herself as "Dorothy Chestnut" and claimed that she was the only child of Chesnut's deceased brother.Using that identity, the person agreed to sell the house to Ultra Home Solutions, LLC. The transaction was handled by Rudy Title and Escrow, LLC, which had been named as the buyer's closing attorney.The supposed seller provided documents intended to establish her right to the property. Among them were two affidavits stating that Upchurch had died unmarried and without a will, leaving Dorothy Chestnut as his only legal heir. An Arizona driving licence carrying the same name was also submitted.The paperwork further authorised John Gleaves, an employee of Rudy Title, to sign the documents required to complete the sale on behalf of the person claiming ownership.The house was transferred to Ultra Home Solutions in January 2020. The transfer was recorded with Sumner County authorities. Over the following months, the property was sold twice more.After returning to the US and learning about the transactions, Chesnut contacted the police. The investigation eventually led to Podczervinski, who had previously lived in the house with Chesnut's permission, pleading guilty to the property theft.During the subsequent civil proceedings, both sides accepted that Dorothy Chestnut was not a genuine person involved in the inheritance.Chesnut sued company handling the saleChesnut approached the Sumner County Circuit Court in August 2022, seeking to have her ownership legally recognised. She named the title company, the original buyer, Gleaves and later purchasers in her case.She argued that the fraudulent transaction could have been detected if the title company had examined the records of her brother's estate before proceeding with the sale.Those records, she maintained, would have identified the people legally entitled to inherit Upchurch's property. She accused Rudy Title of negligence in preparing the transaction and also alleged fraudulent conduct. Her lawsuit sought damages of at least $1 million.The proceedings against the other parties were later dismissed or withdrawn, leaving Rudy Title as the remaining defendant.The company denied that it owed Chesnut a legal duty of care. Its position was that she had no contractual relationship with the firm, which had been involved in completing the transaction for the buyer.In March 2025, the circuit court ruled in favour of Rudy Title. It concluded that Chesnut had not shown that she relied on information or actions provided by the company in managing her own affairs. The court dismissed her entire case.What Appeals court saidChesnut challenged the dismissal, arguing that the company should not have escaped legal scrutiny over its role in the transaction.The Tennessee Court of Appeals examined her arguments but found problems with the way her negligence case had been presented. Some legal grounds she relied on during the appeal had not been raised before the circuit court. Another argument had not been sufficiently developed or supported. As a result, the appeals court left the dismissal of the negligence claim unchanged.The fraud allegation, however, presented a separate issue. The judges found that Rudy Title had asked the lower court to dismiss the negligence claim without addressing Chesnut's accusation of intentional fraudulent conduct.The circuit court had nevertheless dismissed the whole lawsuit, including the allegation that had not been examined in the company's request.The appeals court found that this was improper and restored the fraud portion of Chesnut's case. It directed the lower court to conduct further proceedings.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Accenture CEO Julie Sweet buys 12,200 shares, reveals SEC filing; here's what makes the purchase 'notable'
articles.summary: Accenture CEO Julie Sweet has purchased 12,200 shares of the company on October 26, 2026.
articles.body: Accenture CEO Julie Sweet has purchased 12,200 shares of the company on October 26, 2026. According to a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Julie Sweet now owns 48,910 shares of the company. What makes the purchase notable is that it runs against the broader insider pattern at Accenture over the past year. An analysis by GuruFocus reveals that there have been 2 insider buys in total over the past year, compared with 25 insider sells over the same timeframe. “For Julie Sweet specifically, the past-year record shows 12,200 shares purchased in total and 28,168 shares sold in total. The latest buy therefore adds to the insider's purchases but does not fully offset the prior sales,” the financial research platform said.What is insider buying and sellingInsider buying and selling refers to the buying or selling of a company's shares by people who have access to important non-public information about the company, such as its executives, directors or major shareholders. In Julie Sweet’s case, the insider bought shares at a time when the stock has been trading well below the estimate of intrinsic value, which gives the transaction additional context.“At the same time, the heavy balance of sells over the past year (25 sells versus 2 buys across all insiders) means the latest purchase is a single data point within a mixed insider picture rather than a broad-based signal of insider accumulation,” the report stated.Accenture expands its AI and data workforceIn another news, Accenture said last month that it is expanding its artificial intelligence (AI) and data workforce as it prepares for the next phase of growth. Accenture CEO Julie Sweet then said that the company is already absorbing AI-driven efficiencies in its business, even as clients remain cautious about spending. Speaking at the company’s investor day, Julie Sweet said:“We're absorbing AI efficiencies in our business. We also have a macro that's contributing to a challenging spending environment, and as we look forward, what we actually achieve will, of course, reflect what's happening in the macro”. “But we're not waiting for a meaningful tailwind,” Sweet added.Accenture has grown its AI and data workforce to nearly 110,000 from 40,000, reflecting the growing role of the technology in its operations and services. The company now aims to achieve high-single-digit revenue growth from fiscal year 2029, while using productivity gains to support expansion and improve margins.You use AI every day. articles.title: Indian Navy to get 8 home-designed warships in Rs 53,866 crore deal: What sets them apart
articles.summary: The defence ministry has signed contracts worth Rs 53,866.50 crore for eight Next Generation Corvettes (NGCs) for the Indian Navy.
articles.body: The defence ministry has signed contracts worth Rs 53,866.50 crore for eight Next Generation Corvettes (NGCs) for the Indian Navy. The agreements were inked in New Delhi in the presence of defence secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh. Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers (GRSE) will build five of the ships, and Goa Shipyard Limited (GSL) the remaining three.What sets the project apart is who drew the ships. This is the first time the vessels have been designed in-house by the Indian Navy and then built by Defence Public Sector Undertakings (DPSUs) picked through a competitive process. The project goes back to June 2022, when it first came before the Defence Acquisition Council at a cost of around Rs 36,000 crore. The Cabinet Committee on Security cleared it only days before the signing, at a reported figure of over Rs 40,000 crore. The ministry's announcement does not explain the difference from the contract value.A modern corvetteTraditionally, a corvette is the smallest vessel rated as a warship, between 500 and 2,000 tonnes, built for coastal patrol and fast attack. The NGCs go well beyond that. At a displacement of 3,800 to 4,000 tonnes, they overlap with smaller frigates. They are expected to do more than 30 knots, with a range of 4,000 nautical miles at 14 knots, and will carry 160 sailors and 21 officers.The armament includes a 76 mm super rapid gun mount made by BHEL, eight surface-to-surface missiles, 24 anti-missile defence weapons and two triple 324 mm torpedo tubes. The sensor suite covers surface, air and fire-control radars, an infrared search and track system, a hull-mounted sonar, an active towed array sonar and a combat management system. That mix lets the ships work across the air, surface and sub-surface domains.Replacing an ageing fleetThe ships will replace the Khukri-class corvettes, of which INS Kuthar and INS Khanjar remain in service, and the four Kora-class vessels still with the Navy. Their roles will include protecting maritime trade routes, anti-surface and anti-submarine warfare, coastal defence, littoral combat and surveillance.Beyond the Navy, the ministry points to the industrial effect. The build is expected to generate about 72 lakh person-days of work in the shipyards and 460 lakh person-days in ancillary industries and MSMEs over ten years. With a push for Made-in-India materials, equipment and technology, the programme is being presented as a step towards Aatmanirbharta in defence manufacturing.The first ship is targeted for delivery by 2030, which leaves a long road ahead. For now, the contract settles a question the Navy has been working on for four years: whether an Indian design and Indian public sector yards can deliver a frigate-sized warship at scale.

articles.title: Meet Connor Arbach, the 13-year-old from North Dakota who turned a bag of seasoned pretzels into a homemade snack business, selling his own flavours for $2 a bag
articles.summary: A bag of pretzels became the starting point for a small business in Fargo, North Dakota, where Connor Arbach began making his own versions of the familiar
articles.body: A bag of pretzels became the starting point for a small business in Fargo, North Dakota, where Connor Arbach began making his own versions of the familiar snack. According to the North Dakota Department of Agriculture, at 12, he was developing flavours, preparing batches and finding customers willing to pay $2 for a bag of his seasoned creations. What started as an interest in making pretzels has since taken shape as Twistology Pretzels, a youth-owned business with a growing selection of flavours. Connor remains involved in the work behind each packet, from experimenting with ingredients to getting the finished snacks ready for sale. His family helps with the business, which has begun appearing at local markets and community events around the Fargo-Moorhead area.How 13-year-old Connor Arbach turned homemade pretzels into a small businessTwistology Pretzels is based in Fargo, North Dakota, and is built around a relatively simple product: crunchy pretzels coated in homemade seasonings. Connor has developed a range of homemade seasonings, combining familiar savoury flavours with sweeter and spicier options.The business is run by Connor, who was 12 when he began developing the idea, with his family providing support behind the scenes. His involvement extends beyond choosing which flavours to sell. He takes part in preparing the recipes, seasoning the pretzels, baking them and packing the finished products.From ranch and dill pickle to sweet twisted churro pretzelsThe range at Twistology includes familiar savoury combinations alongside flavours that take pretzels in a different direction. Ranch and Dill Pickle are among the more recognisable options, while Zesty Pizza, Honey Mustard, Chili Lime and Chipotle Barbecue offer other combinations of seasoning.There is also Twisted Churro, a sweeter option that draws on the flavour of the popular cinnamon-sugar-coated pastry. The selection gives customers a choice between tangy, spicy, savoury and sweet varieties without moving away from the basic pretzel.Homemade seasoning is central to the product. Each batch is prepared with the intention of giving the pretzels a distinct coating, rather than simply offering the familiar salted version found in most shops.How Connor Arbach sells his $2 pretzel bags at local marketsAccording to WDAY Radio, Connor initially sold his homemade pretzels for $2 a bag, leaving them in the breakroom at his mother's workplace giving customers a straightforward way to try the different varieties. The company has been taking its products to local markets, pop-up stalls and community events across the Fargo-Moorhead area.People attending markets can see the products, choose from the available flavours and purchase them directly. For Connor, selling the snacks is also part of running the business. Making a product is only one stage of the process; getting it packaged and in front of potential buyers is another. The local events give Twistology an opportunity to build familiarity with its name and introduce its different flavours to people in the area.A family-supported business run by a young entrepreneurAlthough Connor is the person behind Twistology, he does not operate entirely on his own. His family helps with the business behind the scenes, supporting the work involved in preparing and selling the pretzels.Connor, however, remains closely involved in the product itself. Recipe development, seasoning, baking and packaging are all among the tasks he handles. Twistology remains a small business rooted in its local community. Its presence at Fargo-area markets and events has given it a way to introduce its products to customers while continuing to develop its range.For Connor, that idea has become a business bearing its own name, with several flavours and a $2 price tag attached to each bag.You use AI every day. articles.title: US midterm elections 2026: What they are, why they matter and when results will be out
articles.summary: The US midterm elections are nationwide elections held every two years, halfway through a president's four-year term.
articles.body: The US midterm elections are nationwide elections held every two years, halfway through a president's four-year term. This year's elections will take place on November 3 with voters choosing members of Congress as well as several state and local officials.Unlike presidential elections, midterms do not decide who occupies the White House. Instead, they determine which party controls Congress for the next two years, making them a crucial test of President Donald Trump's political standing and his ability to push through his agenda.What are the US midterm elections?The US Congress has two chambers, the House of Representatives and the Senate, and midterm elections determine the composition of both. All 435 seats in the House are contested every two years, as members serve two-year terms.In the Senate, where members serve six-year terms, roughly one-third of the 100 seats come up for election every two years. This time, 35 Senate seats, including two special-election contests, are at stake. Alongside congressional races, voters in several states will also elect governors and other state and local officials.What is at stake in the 2026 midterms?Republicans currently hold narrow majorities in both chambers of Congress.The 435-member House has 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, one independent who caucuses with Republicans and two vacant seats. A party needs 218 seats for a majority.Meanwhile, the Senate has 53 Republicans and 47 Democrats and allied independents, with 51 seats required for a majority. Democrats need a net gain of four seats in each chamber to take control of both.The outcome could therefore hinge on a small number of closely contested races.Why do the midterms matter for Trump?The party controlling Congress has considerable influence over the president's ability to govern.Congress passes legislation, approves government spending and oversees the executive branch. The Senate also confirms presidential nominees to key government positions, including federal judges and senior administration officials.If Democrats take control of either chamber, they could make it harder for Trump to pass legislation, influence budget negotiations and intensify congressional scrutiny of his administration through hearings and investigations.A Democratic majority in the House could also revive discussions of impeachment, although impeachment by itself would not remove the president from office. Removal requires a two-thirds vote in the Senate.Trump would remain president regardless of the election outcome. He would retain his executive powers and the ability to veto legislation, but a divided Congress could significantly constrain his domestic agenda.What issues are shaping the vote?The cost of living, inflation, immigration and the economy are among the major concerns for voters. Foreign policy, including the war involving Iran, is also part of the political debate.Trump's approval ratings and public perceptions of his administration's performance are likely to influence the results. Midterm elections are often viewed as a referendum on the sitting president, with the party in the White House frequently losing congressional seats.Disputes over voting rules, election administration and the drawing of congressional district boundaries have also become contentious issues.When will voting take place and when will results come?Voting will take place on Tuesday, November 3, across the United States. Polling hours vary by state, and there is no single nationwide closing time.The first polling stations in parts of Indiana and Kentucky are scheduled to close at 6 pm Eastern Time, which is around 4.30 am on November 4 as per Indian Standard Time.Results are expected to emerge through the night, but close contests may take longer to resolve. Election officials must count outstanding ballots, verify results and, where necessary, conduct recounts or deal with legal challenges.News organisations may project winners before every ballot has been counted. Such projections are not official results. State election authorities certify the final results, a process that can take days or weeks.Where can you check the results?US Election Assistance Commission (EAC): A federal agency that provides election information and links to official state election offices.USA.gov: The US government's official portal, which directs users to state websites for election results and voting information.Federal Election Commission (FEC): The federal agency responsible for campaign finance oversight. It provides information on federal elections but does not publish live results or certify current election outcomes.State election offices remain the primary source for official results, including vote counts, recounts and final certification.What happens if an election result is contested?A close result can lead to recounts, court challenges and disputes over ballot validity. State officials handle the initial counting and certification process, but the US Constitution gives the House and Senate the power to judge the elections, returns and qualifications of their own members.A candidate or sitting member can challenge a congressional election result. In the House, such disputes are referred to the House Administration Committee, while Senate challenges go to the Senate Rules Committee. The respective chamber ultimately decides whether a member should be seated.This power could become significant if a handful of unresolved races determine which party controls Congress. Any House contests still unresolved when the new Congress convenes in January would be considered by the incoming House.The process can become politically contentious, particularly when party control is at stake. A disputed result may also leave a seat vacant while legal or congressional proceedings continue.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: US midterms 2026: Trump calls Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed a ‘jihadist’ at Iowa rally, hails Republican Mike Rogers as 'apple pie'
articles.summary: During a campaign rally in Iowa, Donald Trump labels Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed a 'jihadist' while endorsing Republican Mike Rogers as 'apple pie'. The remarks come ahead of the critical midterm elections that could determine control of the Senate.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump targeted Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed at a campaign rally in Iowa on Sunday, repeatedly calling the Michigan progressive a “jihadist” and making remarks about his Muslim faith as voters prepare to head to the polls for Tuesday’s midterm elections.Trump's comments came as El-Sayed remains in a closely contested Michigan Senate race against Republican candidate Mike Rogers. The result could influence which party controls the Senate after the elections.“If you vote for this jihadist lunatic that wants to destroy you, you’re crazy,” Trump told the crowd. He also said Congress would need to “get a special metal detector for Abdul” if the candidate were elected.The Michigan contest has attracted national attention following a dispute between El-Sayed and fellow Democrat Haley Stevens, who lost to him in the August primary. Stevens had refused to campaign alongside the nominee and called on him to distance himself from an advertisement by an outside political group. The advertisement linked rising prices to US military support for Israel's war in Gaza.El-Sayed subsequently asked Stevens not to attend a campaign event where the two were scheduled to appear together on Sunday. Stevens instead endorsed Rogers, prompting criticism from Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer.Trump praised Stevens for backing the Republican candidate and encouraged her to join the GOP.“It was an incredible thing,” he said. “I’d love her to join the Republican party. I think that could happen.”The president also endorsed Rogers, describing him as “apple pie” and contrasting the Republican candidate with what he called “communists or jihadists” and the Muslim Brotherhood.“Mike Rodgers is apple pie. And you know what this country needs? A little apple pie. We don’t need the communists or jihadists, the Muslim Brotherhood. We need apple pie. He’s apple pie. He’ll be good,” Trump said.Trump also used the rally to underline the importance he attached to the midterm elections, urging supporters to view the contest as a test of his own presidency.He said he had spent much of the weekend travelling to campaign events instead of watching football.“Pretend I’m on the ballot,” Trump told the crowd, adding: “Essentially, I am on the ballot.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Ukraine defies Trump, puts Russian oil refineries back in the firing line
articles.summary: Ukraine has resumed drone attacks on Russian oil refineries despite US President Donald Trump's efforts to persuade Kyiv to halt strikes on Moscow's
articles.body: Ukraine has resumed drone attacks on Russian oil refineries despite US President Donald Trump's efforts to persuade Kyiv to halt strikes on Moscow's energy infrastructure, signalling growing differences between Washington and Kyiv over the conduct of the Russia-Ukraine war.According to a report by The Guardian, citing Russian state media, Ukrainian long-range drones set fire to the Kstovo oil refinery in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region overnight on Sunday. The attack followed another strike on the Rosneft-owned Novokuybyshevsk refinery in the Samara region on Friday.Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent that Kyiv had never agreed to a proposed 30-day suspension of attacks on Russian oil refineries, which was reportedly conveyed by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared KushnerUkrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has defended strikes on Russian targets, arguing that Kyiv is responding to Moscow's continued attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure.In a post on Telegram, Zelenskyy said Russian drone and ballistic missile attacks had targeted four Ukrainian regions overnight, leaving hundreds of thousands of households without electricity. He accused Moscow of exploiting Ukraine's shortage of ballistic missile interceptors, saying the intensity of Russian strikes remained extremely high.Russia, meanwhile, accused Ukraine of disregarding US efforts to halt attacks on energy infrastructure. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Kyiv was continuing its strikes despite Washington's position. Moscow has maintained that Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities undermine efforts to reach a negotiated settlement.The latest strikes are part of Ukraine's wider campaign targeting Russia's oil infrastructure, which has intensified during the war.Kyiv has repeatedly targeted refineries, oil depots and export facilities using long-range drones to disrupt Russian fuel supplies, damage refining capacity and put pressure on an important source of revenue for Moscow. These facilities also supply petroleum products used by Russia's armed forces, making them strategically significant targets.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Imran Khan tenders unconditional apology in HC over anti-SIR protest participation
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Actor Imran Khan on Monday tendered an unconditional apology after the Bombay high court reprimanded him for participating in a protest against
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Actor Imran Khan on Monday tendered an unconditional apology after the Bombay high court reprimanded him for participating in a protest against the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls despite being a US citizen.A bench led by Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra questioned how the United States would have reacted if an Indian national had protested there."What for were you there? There's a complete difference between the rights of citizens and OCI card holders... You need to clarify whether you were there for protests or for some other work. You will have to categorically make a statement that you had no association with the protests, etc. Because the agitation was with regard to SIR, with which you have no concern at all," the court said."Obviously, because you aren't an Indian citizen... Imagine if an Indian citizen does such protests in any other country, take, for example, your country - the US. That Indian citizen would have been sent back to the country on the next immediate flight," the court added.Following Khan's apology, the Bombay high court scheduled the next hearing for December 7 and kept the "Leave India" notice against him in abeyance until then.The Bombay high court was hearing Khan's plea challenging a Leave India Notice (LIN) issued by the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO), directing him to leave India by October 28. The court had earlier kept the notice in abeyance until November 2 and has now extended the relief until December 7.Khan, a US citizen and Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) cardholder, was issued the notice on October 14, days after he was detained during a protest against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar in Mumbai on October 10.Following his detention, BJP leader Kirit Somaiya filed a police complaint alleging that Khan had violated OCI rules and visa conditions. The Mumbai Police subsequently forwarded an "unproven" FIR to the FRRO, which then issued the Leave India Notice.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A charity founder stole millions meant for struggling families and spent $320,000 on restaurants; he also put a bartender and his housekeeper on a fake board of directors
articles.summary: The founder of a New York charity established to help low-income families has been sentenced to 8 years in prison after stealing more than $2.5 million in
articles.body: The founder of a New York charity established to help low-income families has been sentenced to 8 years in prison after stealing more than $2.5 million in donations to fund an expensive personal lifestyle. Keith Taylor, who led the Modest Needs Foundation, used money intended for people struggling with unexpected bills to pay for luxury accommodation, costly restaurant meals, food deliveries and other personal expenses. He also created a fake board of directors, listing people including a bartender and his housekeeper without their knowledge, to make his spending appear authorised.How did the charity founder steal millions meant for struggling familiesAccording to the US Department of Justice, Taylor founded Modest Needs in 2002 with the aim of helping low-income individuals and families facing unexpected financial difficulties. The charity operated through a crowdfunding model, allowing donors to contribute towards essential expenses that people living from one pay cheque to the next could not afford.Its support was intended for situations such as unexpected medical bills and repairs to broken household appliances. The organisation focused on people who were working but had little financial security when an emergency arose.However, prosecutors said Taylor gradually turned the charity's finances towards his own needs. The Department of Justice's October 28, 2026 sentencing announcement stated that he had embezzled more than $2.5 million from the organisation and its donors since at least 2015.The earlier criminal complaint, announced by the US Attorney's Office on June 11, 2024, placed the alleged period of theft between 2016 and May 2024. It described how donations intended to provide short-term financial assistance were instead used to maintain Taylor's lifestyle.The Associated Press reported that the charity had attracted attention for its small-scale approach to philanthropy, allowing donors to see how their contributions could directly help individuals facing financial problems.Where did the stolen charity money goThe money was spent on a range of personal luxuries, with expensive restaurant visits accounting for a substantial portion of the stolen funds.According to the Department of Justice, Taylor spent more than $320,000 of charity money at some of New York City's most expensive restaurants and steakhouses. These included Per Se, Jean-Georges, Masa and Marea. He reportedly visited these establishments regularly, sometimes dining out twice in a single day.AP highlighted the prices associated with some of the restaurants. Marea's menu included a dry-aged ribeye costing $240, while Per Se offered a nine-course tasting menu priced at $390.Restaurant bills were only part of the spending. More than $300,000 of the charity's money went towards rent for Taylor's luxury apartment on the 30th floor of a Manhattan skyscraper.He also spent over $100,000 on food delivery services and used charitable funds to purchase expensive electronic devices. The money was also used to cover his personal medical expenses, including cosmetic surgery.The Justice Department further revealed that Taylor transferred more than $270,000 directly into his personal brokerage account. He also routinely paid other personal bills using the charity's bank accounts.Taylor used a fake board to hide the spendingProsecutors said Taylor attempted to conceal the misuse of donations by creating a fake board of directors. He claimed that the board had approved his personal expenses and provided oversight of the organisation's finances.However, the people named as board members had no knowledge of their supposed positions. According to the Justice Department, Taylor used the names of acquaintances and listed them on the charity's website and tax documents as members of its governing board.Those individuals included a bartender at Jean-Georges, a friend and his housekeeper. None of them had attended a board meeting or even knew that their names were being used in this way.The arrangement allowed Taylor to create the appearance that his financial decisions had been reviewed and authorised by others, even though the people named had no involvement in the charity's management.What happened after the investigation beganTaylor's activities came under federal investigation, leading to his arrest on June 11, 2024. The initial complaint accused him of embezzling approximately $2.5 million, committing tax offences and using other people's identities as part of the scheme.The criminal case also involved allegations of tax evasion. According to the original Justice Department announcement, Taylor had failed to file personal income tax returns or pay taxes on money received from the charity for at least the calendar years 2017 through 2022. Prosecutors said this resulted in more than $1 million in unpaid federal income taxes.Taylor continued using the charity's money even after his arrest in June 2024. The Justice Department said he had purportedly resigned from his position and was no longer supposed to have access to the organisation's bank accounts under the conditions of his pretrial release.Despite those restrictions, he continued using the funds for personal expenses, including meals, medical bills and rent. The department said these actions also violated the conditions of his release.What punishment did the charity founder receiveTaylor eventually pleaded guilty to the charges on August 18, 2025. On October 28, 2026, US District Judge Jennifer L Rochon sentenced the 59-year-old to 8 years in prison.The sentence also included three years of supervised release after his imprisonment. He was ordered to pay $3,118,237 in forfeiture and $4,144,645 in restitution. The case was investigated by the Internal Revenue Service's Criminal Investigation division and special agents from the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York.You use AI every day. articles.title: Palantir’s Alex Karp is now a forest owner: Buys 37,000 acres in Sweden for reported $22 million; why hunters can no longer enter it
articles.summary: Palantir CEO Alex Karp has purchased 15,000 hectares (37,000 acres) of forest in Härjedalen, Sweden, through his newly registered company Cladonia Skog AB.
articles.body: Palantir CEO Alex Karp has purchased 15,000 hectares (37,000 acres) of forest in Härjedalen, Sweden, through his newly registered company Cladonia Skog AB. As reported by Swedish newspaper Tidningen Härjedalen, the sale was reportedly for 235 million kronor, or $22 million. As per the report, hunters in the region had received notifications in the mail alerting them they could no longer lease the land to hunt south of the quiet village of Storsjö Kapell, known for its hiking and fishing. The sale was later confirmed by Svenska Cellulosa Aktiebolaget (SCA), a paper manufacturer that previously owned the land.Why hunters can no longer enter the forest that Alex Karp boughtIn an emailed statement to Fortune then, SCA spokesperson Robert Östholm said: “We grant hunting rights through lease agreements with a term of approximately 11 months. This means that the agreements can be reviewed and renewed on an annual basis”.“As we have now sold the land in question, we can of course no longer grant hunting rights on it, as the land is no longer owned by us”.Jenny Lopes Da Silva, a board member of Cladonia and a sales manager at Scandinavian Trust, said in a statement said “The new owner of the forest property is committed to the beauty of the land and its preservation. You remain PM because of foreign help. Your financial system is fully controlled and supported by foreigners. This is not opposition; this is obstruction,” he added.In a veiled reference to Rahul's foreign trips, he said, “Due to the frustration of more than a decade, these people have now come out in the open. articles.title: After losing The Traitors, Alexander Dragonetti inspired thousands to donate £95,000 to a charity that supported his late brother
articles.summary: Alexander Dragonetti did not win the third series of the BBC reality show The Traitors, but his appearance inspired an extraordinary response from viewers.
articles.body: Alexander Dragonetti did not win the third series of the BBC reality show The Traitors, but his appearance inspired an extraordinary response from viewers. After sharing the story of his late brother, James, who had a learning disability and autism, the former British diplomat inspired thousands of people to donate to Mencap, a UK charity that had supported his family. Dragonetti had said he wanted to donate some of his potential prize money to the organisation in tribute to his brother. Although he left the competition without the winnings, viewers rallied around the cause. Donations initially reached around £30,000 before climbing further, with Mencap announcing in April 2025 that the fundraising total had reached approximately £95,000. The charity later recorded £96,556 raised through the campaign.How Dragonetti's brother inspired the fundraisingDragonetti spoke about his brother James during the third series of The Traitors, explaining the importance of the support his family had received. James had global developmental delay and autism, and he died at the age of 17, when Alexander was 24.Mencap had supported James through its summer camps, which gave him opportunities to spend time with others. Dragonetti also volunteered at the camps, which provided families with a break from their caring responsibilities. He described the experience as meaningful for both his brother and his family.Dragonetti said he wanted to support the charity because of the difference it had made to his brother and family. His decision to speak publicly about James brought attention to the experiences of families caring for people with learning disabilities and helped direct viewers towards Mencap.Donations rose rapidly after the show's finalThe fundraising response gathered pace after the series finale aired in January 2025. On January 27, Mencap reported that it had received more than 2,000 donations, bringing the total to around £30,000. Sky News subsequently reported that the donations had reached £31,000.The response continued to grow. By January 31, donations had exceeded £70,000, according to Sky News. On April 10, 2025, Mencap announced that around £95,000 had been raised following Dragonetti's appearance on the programme.Mencap's fundraising impact report for 2024-25 later recorded a total of £96,556, raised through 5,510 cash donors and 196 regular givers. The charity said some of the funds would support respite activities similar to the summer camp James had attended.Dragonetti joined Mencap as an official supporterOn April 10, 2025, Mencap announced that Dragonetti had become an official high-profile supporter. The charity also released a video showing him making surprise calls to people who had donated after hearing his story, thanking them for their generosity and asking what had motivated them to contribute.Dragonetti said the fundraising response had been incredible and stressed that he wanted to do more than raise money. He also wanted to increase awareness of learning disabilities, challenge stigma and promote greater understanding and inclusion.During the calls, he heard from donors about their own experiences of learning disabilities and how the issue had affected their families. He said hearing their stories was humbling and often moving, even during brief conversations.Mencap chief executive Jon Sparkes welcomed Dragonetti's support, saying that sharing his family's story had helped raise awareness and encouraged people to understand the experiences of those with learning disabilities.What is Mencap, and how does it support families?Mencap is a UK charity that supports people with learning disabilities and their families. Its work includes providing direct support, campaigning for better services and opportunities, challenging discrimination and promoting greater inclusion.The charity says around 1.5 million people in the UK have a learning disability. It campaigns for their rights and works to improve access to health and social care, employment opportunities and support for families.The money raised following Dragonetti's appearance helped fund Mencap's work, including respite activities for people with learning disabilities and their families. Such activities can offer participants opportunities to socialise and take part in experiences outside their usual routines, while giving family carers time to rest.His story resonated with viewersThe response extended beyond the initial wave of donations. Mencap published messages from people who said Dragonetti's story had encouraged them to contribute, including parents of children with learning disabilities and people whose families had benefited from similar support. Some donors said they had given specifically because of his appearance on the programme.The charity said sharing the experiences of people with learning disabilities and their loved ones can help change attitudes and make society more inclusive. Dragonetti's story also highlighted the role that respite services and community activities can play in supporting families.Although Dragonetti did not win The Traitors, his tribute to James prompted a substantial fundraising response. What began as his intention to donate some of his potential prize money became a public campaign that raised nearly £100,000 for the charity that had supported his brother.You use AI every day. articles.title: Ukraine has 500 Patriot missiles on order, but Russia's winter offensive exposes a critical supply gap
articles.summary: Due to the ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and West Asia, air defence stockpiles around the world are being depleted faster than factories can replenish them.
articles.body: Due to the ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and West Asia, air defence stockpiles around the world are being depleted faster than factories can replenish them. Russia continues to fire ballistic missiles and drones at Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure, while sustained operations in West Asia have drawn down stocks of similar weapons in other parts of the world.The interceptors at the centre of this problem were designed in an era when militaries expected short-duration but intense conflicts and did not anticipate firing such weapons in large numbers. These air defence missiles were expected to be used largely against combat aircraft and occasional surface-to-surface missiles.The proliferation of drones and cruise missiles, along with the growing use of ballistic missiles, has changed air defence dynamics. Under these new conditions, Ukraine's need for the Patriot system's most advanced interceptor is now running up against the pace of American production of PAC-3 missiles, which are seeing a massive surge in demand.On October 30, the US State Department approved a possible sale of 500 PAC-3 MSE interceptors to Ukraine, valued at an estimated $2.1 billion. The US is not funding this procurement. Instead, the purchase is to be financed by Canada, Germany and Norway through the US JUMPSTART programme, alongside funding linked to the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan, with Lockheed Martin as the primary contractor. The deal comes just before the onset of an extremely cold winter, with Russia targeting Ukrainian power infrastructure to put pressure on Kyiv.An approval is not a deliveryThe approval is an important step, but it does not mean 500 missiles are sitting in a warehouse. It is clearance for a possible sale, and the missiles still have to be built, tested and shipped. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that they may not arrive for several years, even though Kyiv needs interceptors for the coming winter. Reuters, citing two sources, reported that the newly approved missiles are not expected until the 2030s.A procurement decision cannot refill an air defence magazine emptied in combat, and that gap between paperwork and delivery is at the heart of the story.The recently approved sale of 500 Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement interceptors to Ukraine by the Americans, is a typical example of what can befall a country that relies heavily on import of defence stores to fight its wars. The deal for the Patriot missiles will take years to roll out, while the threat to Ukraine is immediate. In fact, Zelensky has already approached the US for faster deliveries. The defence industry takes time to grow its roots and develop a domestic eco-system. In fact, Zelenskyy has often been forced to modulate his war plans in consonance with limitations imposed by his war fighting inventory, restrictions imposed by supplier nations and such like factors. These limitations have adversely affected the course of battles Ukrainians have fought. In today’s world, technological superiority, and the ability to manufacture cutting edge platforms are an integral component of military capability of a nation. The more self-reliant the State is, better is it for its sovereign decision making.The factory floorTo understand the gap, it helps to look at what Lockheed Martin can actually build. The company delivered a record 620 PAC-3 MSE interceptors in 2025. In January 2026, the firm announced a seven-year framework agreement with the US government to raise annual production capacity from roughly 600 missiles to 2,000, more than a threefold increase.If output continues at the 2025 pace, an order of 500 missiles would equal about 81% of a full year's output. If production eventually reaches 2,000 missiles a year, the same order would equal about three months of production.Neither figure is a delivery forecast, because Lockheed Martin also supplies the US military and several international customers, and a factory's annual output is not the same as the number of missiles available for export.Why 500 missiles can take yearsThere are three constraints at work here. The first is the manufacturing cycle. The New Voice of Ukraine reported that producing one missile can take as long as 24 months. That does not mean each missile sits on the production line for two years, since work on different missiles overlaps and components are made in parallel. It does mean an order for hundreds of advanced interceptors cannot be filled like an order for a standard commercial product.The second is competition for the same missiles. The US armed forces need PAC-3 interceptors, as do America's European, West Asian and Indo-Pacific allies that operate Patriot systems. Any increase in production has to serve this wider demand, not just Ukraine.The third is the industrial base behind the final assembly line. Missiles depend on a network of suppliers, specialised components, skilled workers, testing facilities and manufacturing equipment. Lockheed Martin's expansion agreement is designed to grow capacity across that network, but the investment takes time to translate into completed, tested missiles.In effect, the 500-missile sale is a long-term replenishment measure and does not answer how Ukraine will defend its cities before the new production arrives.How long would 500 missiles last?The pressure on stocks becomes clearer when set against Ukraine's own estimates of what it needs. In September, Defense Express reported Zelenskyy's estimate that Ukraine would need 100 to 120 ballistic-missile interceptors every month during the coming winter. On October 24, Kyiv Post reported Zelenskyy as saying Ukraine had received just 24 Patriot interceptors from the United States over the previous three months.The arithmetic is sobering for decision-makers in Kyiv. At 100 interceptors a month, 500 missiles would last five months; at 120 a month, about four months.These are illustrative calculations, not forecasts, since they assume all 500 missiles are available on day one and that consumption remains constant. Actual usage would depend on the number and type of incoming missiles, the number of operational Patriot batteries and the availability of other air defence systems.Not every Russian missile needs a PAC-3 MSE, and using these scarce, expensive interceptors against threats that cheaper systems can handle would only deplete stocks faster.PAC-3 Edge: The capability betLockheed Martin's answer is a new variant called the PAC-3 Edge, a more capable future interceptor for the Patriot family. This variant is intended to improve range, altitude and manoeuvrability over the current MSE version.The planned changes include a new seeker, an upgraded control system and a more advanced solid rocket motor developed with Northrop Grumman. It is aimed at more sophisticated threats, including advanced ballistic and hypersonic missiles.Lockheed Martin has said testing is expected to begin in 2027, with initial deployment targeted for 2031. These are programme targets, not proof that the missile is ready.The company plans to build Edge on its existing PAC-3 production line in Camden, Arkansas, with factory modernisation supporting the transition. It says production of the new missile could rise as MSE output tapers off, while retaining the ability to increase production when demand spikes.Steelfin: The volume betAgainst this backdrop, the American defence industry is pursuing two different answers. The first came on October 12, when Anduril unveiled Steelfin, a family of modular surface-to-air missiles.The idea behind the missile is to build a common airframe, avionics, software, flight controls and interfaces, and then vary the booster and terminal-stage components to suit the threat.This family of missiles is meant to cover missions ranging from point defence against aerial threats to lower-tier air and missile defence and some ballistic missile defence roles, with compatibility planned for existing launchers such as the Mk 41 Vertical Launch System (VLS) deployed across US Navy ships and selected Patriot-related equipment.The most consequential claim is about scale. Anduril says it is planning near-term production of several thousand missiles a year, with capacity that can shift towards whichever variant is in demand.The US-based firm has not disclosed a detailed production schedule or contract quantities, and flight testing of Steelfin variants is planned for 2027. The cost comparisons the company has made against more expensive interceptors are likewise company claims, not independently demonstrated results.The logic of modularity is simple: If one design can be adapted for different missions, the manufacturer needs fewer separate production processes and can move between variants without building a new production line.But commonality does not remove every bottleneck. Different seekers, rocket motors and terminal stages still need to be qualified and tested.The bigger lessonAir defence forces need enough missiles to sustain operations and interceptors capable enough to defeat the hardest threats.A cheaper, high-volume interceptor could help preserve the most advanced weapons for targets that require them, while an improved top-end missile would widen the range of threats that can be engaged.The PAC-3 MSE is the only one of the three that is operational today. Steelfin and Edge are both in development, and neither will help Ukraine this winter.That is the larger point: The Patriot shortage is as much a question of industrial speed as it is of money or political will.The capacity expansion from roughly 600 to 2,000 missiles a year is significant, but it will take years to build, while missiles are being used up now.For Ukraine, the near-term question is whether its partners can release interceptors from existing stocks while an expanded production base catches up.The number that matters most is not what a company says it can eventually build, but how many working interceptors it can deliver each month, how fast that rate can rise, and how much of that output reaches the places where it is urgently needed.

articles.title: ‘I’d do it’: Trump says he would consider pre-emptive pardons for all admin staff if Democrats pursue prosecutions
articles.summary: In a recent interview, President Trump expressed willingness to issue pre-emptive pardons for his administration officials if Democrats pursue prosecutions following the midterm elections. He cited past pardons granted to individuals linked to the January 6 Capitol attack and criticized current calls for investigations into his administration.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has said he would consider issuing pre-emptive pardons to people who served in his administration if Democrats pursue criminal cases against them after potentially gaining control of Congress.In an interview with The New York Post's Miranda Devine for her Pod Force One podcast, Trump was asked whether he would grant pardons to protect former and current administration officials from possible prosecution.“I would if I needed to. Sure,” he said.When asked whether the offer would extend to everyone who had worked for him, Trump reaffirmed his position, saying: “I’d do it. I did it for J6.”Trump was referring to his decision to pardon around 1,500 defendants charged in connection with the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol. He signed the pardons on his first day back in office in January 2025.The president also pointed to former President Joe Biden's use of presidential clemency shortly before leaving office. Biden issued pre-emptive pardons to Dr Anthony Fauci, former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Mark Milley, members and staff of the House committee that investigated the January 6 attack, and several members of his family, including his son Hunter Biden.“That’s what Biden did. He gave everybody a pardon,” Trump said.Trump also criticised the congressional committee that investigated the Capitol attack, referring to it as the “unselect committee” and a “corrupt committee”.His comments come amid calls from some Democrats to investigate and prosecute members of the Trump administration if the party gains control of Congress in the midterm elections.Last month, Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan said at an event at the University of Chicago that a Democratic majority should pursue what she described as “signature cases” against people who enabled Trump's administration. She said the prospect of prosecution could discourage young conservatives from accepting government positions.“I want that deterrence message sent,” Slotkin said.In footage recorded by an undercover journalist on Thursday, Slotkin reportedly outlined plans for congressional committees to pursue individual investigations and hold officials accountable from January.Representative Jamie Raskin of Maryland, who could become chairman of the House Judiciary Committee if Democrats win control of the chamber, has also pledged to investigate what he has described as “systemic corruption” within the administration.Other proposals targeting people associated with the administration have also emerged from the political left. Former Labour Secretary Robert Reich has called for Democrats to lay the groundwork for nationalising SpaceX, while some commentators have suggested that staff members of the Department of Government Efficiency, including Edward Coristine, should face scrutiny.During the interview, Devine also raised the possibility that Democrats might target billionaire Elon Musk or seek his arrest. Trump dismissed the prospect, saying: “It won’t happen. It’s talk.”“But if it is talk, we’ll have to protect them,” he added.However, presidential pardons have constitutional limits. They apply to federal offences and cannot prevent state-level prosecutions, civil lawsuits or impeachment proceedings.Asked whether Democrats might also pursue action against him personally, Trump was less certain.“Well, I don’t know about me,” he said.The president also questioned polling that indicated Democrats were favoured to gain control of the House of Representatives. He described the surveys as “rigged” and pointed to attendance at his campaign rallies as evidence that Republicans could perform better than expected.“We’ll know on Tuesday night,” Trump said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Kevin Costner’s Yellowstone brought an estimated 2.1 million visitors to Montana in one year, and a university study links the series to $730 million in tourism spending
articles.summary: Kevin Costner’s Yellowstone television series brought an estimated 2.1 million visitors to Montana in 2021, and a university study links the show to $730
articles.body: Kevin Costner’s Yellowstone television series brought an estimated 2.1 million visitors to Montana in 2021, and a university study links the show to $730 million in spending. Costner plays John Dutton, the sixth-generation patriarch of a fictional Montana ranch family, in a Paramount Network drama described as the most popular series on American television. Filming takes place largely in Darby, Hamilton, Missoula and the Bitterroot Valley. Its season-five premiere showed more than 12 million viewers the scenery of western Montana, and the series was the highest-rated non-sports programme of the 2021-22 season. The audience stretches well beyond the United States.A television drama has arguably eclipsed millions of dollars in state tourism advertisingFilm tourism is the branch of travel in which visitors seek out places made famous by films and television programmes. According to the Montana Economist, it applies especially well to Yellowstone. The show’s title recalls the famously beautiful national park, while its characters, stories, and backdrop embrace the Mountain West and, above all, western Montana's landscape.The Montana Office of Tourism spends millions on advertising campaigns to raise awareness of the state’s attractions. The Montana Economist argues that the popularity of the series has arguably eclipsed those efforts and lifted Montana’s image among a far wider audience of potential travellers.Researchers added a national survey of past visitors to a production study of season fourSince 2020, the series has been filmed entirely in western Montana. The Montana Economist reported that the studio disclosed detailed spending records when applying for a film tax credit under the Montana Economic Development Industry Advancement Act, which became law in July 2019.Researchers at the University of Montana’s Bureau of Business and Economic Research used those records for an April 2022 report. It found that about $72 million of qualifying spending, together with 116 Montana residents employed in production, supported 527 new jobs, $25.3 million in additional personal income and $85.3 million in extra gross receipts. That covered the five months from October 2020 to February 2021, when season four was made.The report admitted a gap, it left out the advertising value of films that use Montana as a backdrop. To fill it, the bureau teamed up with the university’s Institute for Tourism and Recreation Research. Using the survey firm Qualtrics, they assembled a national panel of people who live outside Montana but had visited within the previous three years. Respondents were asked why, how often and for how long they visited, and how far the show influenced their decision.Seven in ten past visitors had watched the show, and nearly one in five said it swayed their tripAmong the surveyed visitors, 71.2% said they had watched Yellowstone, 12.5% were unsure, and 16.2% had not. Because individual episodes draw 10 to 12 million viewers nationally, the researchers noted that this group is far more likely to tune in than the general population.Asked how much the show influenced their decision to travel, 19.3% chose one of the two strongest options on a five-point scale. The researchers combined these answers with the institute’s visitor spending profiles to estimate how much spending the show induced in 2021.A “no Yellowstone” scenario shows more than 10,000 extra jobs and $376 million in household incomeTo judge the overall effect, the researchers built a hypothetical economy in which season four was never filmed and the visitors who said the show motivated their trip never came. Comparing it with the real economy measured what the series adds.The gap was large. The Montana Economist reported more than 10,000 additional jobs statewide, and household income $376.1 million higher, of which $324.7 million was after-tax income available to spend. State tax revenue directed in whole or in part to the general fund rose by $44.5 million, including $17.3 million from the individual income tax.The University of Montana added that the activity generated roughly $1.1 billion in business and nonbusiness output. It also said the $730.1 million figure combines visitor spending with film production spending. Patrick Barkey, director of the bureau, told the University of Montana that extending the earlier analysis to tourism was “eye-opening”.The benefits stretched beyond hotels to health care, transportation, electricians and carpentersAs expected, many of the new jobs sit in industries that receive visitor spending, such as accommodation and food, and arts and entertainment. The Montana Economist found significant job gains in seemingly unrelated sectors too, including health care and transportation, as the money passed from business to business.Todd O’Hair, president and chief executive of the Montana Chamber of Commerce, told the university that food services, hotels, rental companies and transport firms were all benefiting, as were high-tech businesses and skilled trades such as electricians and carpenters. He described the show as a big driver of tourism, jobs and tax revenue. The study also estimated that the higher economic opportunity attracted and kept 3,305 more people in the state.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Man who invaded CEO's mansion in Toronto discharged from hospital after gunshot wound treatment, Cops say 'we did not have evidence then'
articles.summary: Toronto police faced massive criticism after they decided not to arrest the man who was admitted to a hospital with a gunshot wound after he broke into a
articles.body: Toronto police faced massive criticism after they decided not to arrest the man who was admitted to a hospital with a gunshot wound after he broke into a CEO's mansion and grievously injured four family members. Police said they did not have sufficient evidence to take him 23-year-old Daijohn Richards into custody when he was at St. Joseph's Health Centre before he was discharged on Friday afternoon. Officers were not unaware of his presence. They questioned him and then let him go.Hours later, they published the photo of Richards seeking help in his arrest as he was linked to the violent home invasion at the $2.1 million Toronto mansion of real estate executive David Morton, 75.He is now the subject of a Canada-wide arrest warrant, prompting questions about why police did not take him into custody while he was receiving treatment.The decision sparked outrage on social media, with users questioning how a man who had arrived at a hospital with a gunshot wound shortly after a violent home invasion could leave without being arrested.Why did Toronto police not arrest Richards?Toronto Police addressed the controversy on Saturday, saying investigators had immediately recognized the possible connection between the home invasion and the man who had arrived at the hospital with a gunshot wound."We want to address some confusion surrounding the investigation into the home invasion in the Bridle Path neighborhood," the department said in a statement on X."Investigators immediately recognized the potential connection between the home invasion and the individual who showed up at hospital with a gunshot wound."But identifying a potential suspect was not the same as having sufficient evidence to make an arrest, they said."But recognizing a potential suspect and having enough evidence to arrest them are two different things. Suspicion alone isn't enough. Police need reasonable grounds, supported by evidence, to make an arrest," the department said.Police also defended the detectives involved, praising their "professionalism, tenacity and commitment" and saying the investigation was continuing."Let's keep the focus where it belongs: finding the outstanding suspects and holding those responsible for this violent home invasion accountable," the statement added.Inspector Kristy Smith also addressed the issue during a Saturday news conference, acknowledging that questions would arise over why Richards had not been arrested at the hospital."We arrived at the hospital, we made an investigation, and I know the question is going to come about, 'Why did we not arrest him at the time?"' she said.Under Ontario law, hospitals are required to notify police when treating patients with gunshot wounds.Officers went to the hospital and had what Smith described as '"numerous interactions" with Richards. However, investigators had not established reasonable grounds to arrest him at that stage.Detectives subsequently made the connection through forensic investigations and inquiries in the neighbourhood, with assistance from the Centre of Forensic Sciences.By the time investigators had gathered sufficient evidence, Richards was no longer at the hospital.What happened inside the CEO's mansion? Morton's wife was struck with a hammerThe investigation relates to a violent home invasion at the Bridle Path residence of Morton, CEO of Toronto-based real estate company MAC Group.Three masked men armed with firearms and a hammer allegedly forced their way into the property through a rear entrance at around 3.40am on Thursday.Morton, his 64-year-old wife, Doriana Zohil-Morton, and their daughters Maggie, 28, and Cristina, 26, were asleep when the intruders entered their bedrooms and demanded valuables.A violent confrontation followed. Morton and both daughters suffered gunshot wounds, while two members of the family were also struck on the head with a hammer.All four were taken to hospital. Two have since been discharged, while the other two remain under medical care with injuries described as life-altering.Investigators believe Richards was accidentally shot in the right shoulder by one of his alleged accomplices during the confrontation."We believe that he was accidentally shot by one of the other suspects in this home invasion," Smith said.The three attackers fled in a dark-coloured SUV. Police have obtained grainy surveillance images but have not been able to establish the vehicle's make or model.Investigators believe the suspects may have selected the wealthy Bridle Path neighbourhood because of the valuables likely to be found inside its homes, rather than specifically targeting the Morton family.The sprawling property, valued at approximately $2.1 million, features a swimming pool, tennis court and private gardens.Morton previously told the Daily Mail that his family had experienced a "terrifying and life-threatening experience" in the place where they should have felt safest."It is difficult to put into words the trauma of experiencing something so horrific in the one place where everyone should feel safest: their own home," he said."No family should ever have to experience this. People should be able to sleep peacefully in their homes without fear of armed individuals breaking in and threatening their lives."Canada-wide warrant issued for RichardsRichards is wanted on multiple charges, including four counts of discharging a firearm with intent to wound and four counts of robbery with a firearm. He also faces three counts of aggravated assault. Additional charges include breaking and entering, possession of a prohibited device and wearing a disguise with intent.Police have released his photograph and warned that he may be experiencing discomfort from his injured shoulder, which could make him recognisable.Smith issued a direct warning to the fugitive during Saturday's news conference."We know who you are. And we're actively looking for you. Your world just got smaller," she said.The other two masked suspects have not been publicly identified."I want to emphasize that all three suspects are considered armed and dangerous," Smith warned, urging members of the public not to approach them.You use AI every day. articles.title: Meet Brian Troupe, the 16-year-old from Maryland who took his ice cream business onto a boat when selling from a pier failed; by summer 2026, the business had brought in more than $25,000 in gross sales
articles.summary: Sixteen-year-old Brian Troupe turned an unsuccessful pier-side business idea into a floating ice cream business on the Bohemia River in Maryland.
articles.body: Sixteen-year-old Brian Troupe turned an unsuccessful pier-side business idea into a floating ice cream business on the Bohemia River in Maryland. By the end of the 2026 summer season, his boat-based business, Troupe's Treats, had made more than $25,000 in gross sales. The young business owner started his journey at age 15 after a conversation with a neighbour gave him an idea. While they were out on the water, the neighbour mentioned that someone had once sold food to local boaters. Troupe enjoyed spending time on the water and saw a chance to earn some extra money while providing a service that few boaters could access during hot summer days. "I thought quite a bit about how I can kind of sneak past some food certifications and not have to have a sink on a boat and all of this extra equipment," Troupe told Entrepreneur magazine. "And still having something that a lot of boaters don't have on their boat."Setbacks on the shoreTroupe's first attempt to sell ice cream did not go as planned. He set up a small shop at the end of a pier, hoping boaters would stop by to buy frozen treats. However, he did not make a single sale on the first day. Boat owners were unwilling to pull up their anchors and bring their boats alongside the pier. Looking back at that first failure, Troupe told Entrepreneur magazine that it felt like a lemonade stand that had failed. "It went the worst it could have," Troupe said. "Luckily for me, I didn't let that stop me." After realising that customers were unlikely to come to him, Troupe decided to take his business directly to them. He spent around $700 of his own savings on a small jon boat. He also spent another $120 on boat bumpers and basic boating equipment. Rather than waiting at the pier, he travelled to boats anchored on the water and offered pre-packaged ice cream bars for $2 each. The new approach worked straight away. During his first weekend selling directly on the water, Troupe made around $400 in revenue. As the first summer continued, his business averaged $800 per weekend. His best weekend brought in more than $1,200, and he ended the season with almost $6,000 in gross sales.Expansion and upgrades on the waterAfter seeing early success, Troupe expanded his business for the 2026 summer season. He moved from basic store-brand ice cream to more expensive products, including Magnum and Klondike bars. He also increased the price of each item to $3. To handle more customers, Troupe replaced his first boat with a larger Sea-Doo Switch pontoon boat and added a bigger freezer system. These changes allowed Troupe's Treats to cover more areas. The business expanded beyond its original location and began visiting four different anchoring spots across local waterways. The expansion brought a major increase in sales. During the 2026 summer season, the business averaged $1,800 in revenue each weekend. Its highest single-weekend sales went above $2,100. By the end of the season, total gross sales had passed $25,000. Along with selling ice cream, Troupe also introduced his business to local community leaders. According to public records from the Cecilton Town Council, he presented his business model to the council in May 2026. At the time, he was also competing against 63 other participants in a statewide Maryland entrepreneurship contest, which had 64 participants in total.Innovative operational techniquesRunning a shop on open water came with several practical challenges. One of the biggest problems was handing products to customers on boats of different heights. Reaching passengers on larger boats was not always easy. "It becomes a comical scene," Troupe explained to Entrepreneur magazine. To make deliveries easier, Troupe started using long-handled fishing nets with wide hoops. These nets allow him to reach passengers on larger boats and pass them up to six ice cream items at once. Customers then place their cash payments directly into the net. Troupe also came up with a simple way to manage cash payments and change. After increasing the price of each ice cream bar to $3, customers paying with $5 bills often needed two $1 bills in change. To avoid running out of single dollar bills, he began keeping $2 bills on hand to give customers as change. The teenager also offers free "pup cups" to boaters who bring their dogs along. This small extra service helps build good relationships with regular customers and makes the experience more enjoyable for their pets.Future plans and industry adviceLooking ahead, Troupe plans to continue running Troupe's Treats during future summer seasons while keeping his career options open. Although he enjoys owning and running a business, he has long been interested in engineering, especially designing roller coasters for theme parks. He is also open to handing the business over to another young person in the future. "I can even see myself, once I'm a lot older, passing [Troupe's Treats] down to somebody to give another teenager the same opportunity that I had," Troupe told Entrepreneur magazine. "Because this opportunity has really provided me with a lot of education, experience and a lot more than I could have ever thought." When offering advice to other young people who want to start their own businesses, Troupe stresses the importance of not giving up when things go wrong. He believes young entrepreneurs should be ready to make mistakes and learn from them. His main advice is to always leave room for failure, pointing out that the first day at the pier, when he made no money at all, became an important step towards building a successful business.You use AI every day.
