articles.title: In 2014, a New Jersey surfer began selling açai bowls from a roadside cart with less than $5,000; by 2026, Playa Bowls had passed 400 stores after recording $332 million in systemwide sales in 2025
articles.summary: What started as a small homemade food cart on a pavement in New Jersey has grown into a fast-casual restaurant chain with more than 400 locations across
articles.body: What started as a small homemade food cart on a pavement in New Jersey has grown into a fast-casual restaurant chain with more than 400 locations across North America. Playa Bowls was founded in 2014 by local surfers Robert Giuliani and Abby Taylor. In 2026, the company passed the 400-store mark after recording $332 million in total systemwide sales in 2025. Its rapid growth, from a small beachside business to a major national franchise, reflects growing customer interest in healthy and customizable fast-food options.Roots on the Jersey ShoreThe idea for the business came after Giuliani and Taylor spent years travelling to popular surfing destinations, including Panama, Costa Rica, Nicaragua, and Puerto Rico. During their trips, they discovered fruit bowls made with superfoods at small beach huts. They saw a chance to bring the same idea to the American fast-casual market and decided to start a business in their hometown of Belmar, New Jersey. With less than $5,000 to start, the pair built a simple food cart using reclaimed wood, bought a blender, and opened for business outside a local pizza shop on Ocean Avenue. They convinced the building's owner to let them use an outdoor electrical outlet by connecting their extension cord to it. In return, they paid rent for the space. At first, most customers came through recommendations from local surfers and beach visitors. Within a few weeks, people were lining up along the pavement. This encouraged the founders to open their first permanent shop in Belmar later that same year.Rapid franchising and expansionAfter their first beachside locations proved successful, Giuliani and Taylor started offering franchises in 2016. According to figures reported by Entrepreneur magazine, the business grew quickly by focusing on beach towns, college campuses, and shopping areas in suburban neighbourhoods. Unlike traditional fast-food restaurants, Playa Bowls built its identity around a relaxed beach style. Its stores feature hand-painted wall art, neon signs, and decorations inspired by surfing and coastal life. The menu offers customizable bowls made with superfood bases such as açai, pitaya, coconut, chia pudding, and green smoothie blends. Customers can add fresh fruit, nuts, and different toppings and sauces. In 2024, private equity firm Sycamore Partners bought a majority stake in Playa Bowls. The deal provided money to support business growth, improve company operations, and strengthen its supply chain. According to reporting by QSR Magazine, the brand opened dozens of new stores during 2024 and 2025. It also expanded into less traditional locations, including airports, military bases, and stadiums.Financial milestones and operational scaleThe company reached new financial records over the past two financial years. Reporting by Entrepreneur magazine confirms that total systemwide sales reached $332 million in 2025. This growth was supported by strong store performance and steady revenue from individual locations. Franchised stores generated an average of around $1.2 million in annual sales. Some of the best-performing locations in coastal and suburban areas brought in more than $2 million each year. The relatively low cost of opening a Playa Bowls store, compared with restaurants that need large kitchens, has attracted franchise owners who previously operated multiple locations for other major fast-casual brands. Playa Bowls stores mainly need blenders, refrigerators, and food preparation counters. They do not require deep fryers or commercial ovens. This helps keep the cost of setting up a store lower than that of a traditional fast-food restaurant. The simpler setup also allows locations to operate in smaller spaces, usually between 1,200 and 1,800 square feet.Executive leadership and future targetsTo manage its growing network of more than 400 stores, Playa Bowls appointed Dan Rowlands as Chief Executive Officer in late 2024. The founders moved into advisory positions and roles as brand ambassadors. Under the new leadership, the company changed parts of its business structure to support expansion across the country. As reported by QSR Magazine, Playa Bowls has set a target of reaching 800 locations by the end of the decade. Its expansion plans include more stores in the Midwest and on the West Coast. Despite these changes, company leaders say keeping the brand's original identity remains an important part of its growth plans. Stores continue to display local artwork created by in-house artists. This helps maintain the relaxed coastal style that first made the Belmar location stand out. Playa Bowls now operates in more than 35 US states. articles.summary: Pakistan is facing questions over the confidence of its own governing establishment, with defence minister Khawaja Asif alleging that some officials
articles.body: Pakistan is facing questions over the confidence of its own governing establishment, with defence minister Khawaja Asif alleging that some officials holding important positions in the country are planning to settle abroad, including in Portugal and other Western nations.The reported plans have drawn attention to a wider contradiction for the nation grappled with the economic crisis.While the government expects citizens to remain patient amid the country's difficulties, some people within the administration are said to be looking at opportunities and a more secure future overseas for themselves and their families, reported Greek City Times.The issue goes beyond officials moving abroad after retirement as it also raises questions about whether their families are already preparing to build lives elsewhere through overseas education, residency and eventual settlement.If the children of officials study and settle abroad, their families could become less dependent on Pakistan's institutions, even as those officials continue to hold positions of authority at home.The issue of family members studying abroad is also covered in Pakistan's official disclosure requirements. The Establishment Division's asset declaration form asks government officials to provide details of their children's education, including whether they are studying in Pakistan or overseas. It also seeks information about relevant family assets and expenditure.These requirements do not establish how many officials have sent their children abroad or whether they intend to settle overseas. However, they show that such financial arrangements are considered relevant to official disclosure and scrutiny.The reported plans come against the backdrop of a wider migration trend involving Pakistan's educated and professional workforce.In October, overseas Pakistanis minister Chaudhry Salik Hussain told the National Assembly that more than 1.8 million highly educated and professional people had left Pakistan over the previous three years, Pakistan Today reported.The people who moved abroad included doctors, information technology professionals, engineers, academics and skilled workers from several other sectors. Their departure raises concerns about the country's ability to retain experienced professionals across essential industries.The figures cited by the minister underline the scale of the movement of skilled workers out of Pakistan at a time of unprecendented economic crisis.You use AI every day. articles.title: Princess Diana’s homelessness charity now supports more than 15,000 young people each year, with 69% moving towards independent living
articles.summary: Homelessness charities often work with young people at a point when finding somewhere safe to stay is only the beginning of a much longer process.
articles.body: Homelessness charities often work with young people at a point when finding somewhere safe to stay is only the beginning of a much longer process. Securing accommodation does not necessarily mean someone is ready to manage a home, return to education or find work without continued assistance. Centrepoint, the UK charity associated with Princess Diana and now supported by her son, Prince William, works with young people facing these challenges. Its services have expanded considerably since the organisation began in London in 1969. As reported by Centrepoint UK, in 2024/25, it and its partner organisations supported more than 15,000 young people, with its latest figures offering an insight into the help provided and what happens when they leave.Princess Diana’s homelessness charity reaches 15,000 young people in a yearCentrepoint began in 1969 in the basement of a church in Soho, London. The organisation was established to provide a place for young people experiencing homelessness, at a time when the support available to them was limited. The scale of its current work is reflected in its housing provision. Reportedly, Centrepoint operates 90 supported housing services across the UK, with more than 800 bed spaces available to young people. These services are intended to offer more than temporary shelter, giving residents access to support as they work towards greater stability. In 2024/25, the charity and its partner organisations reached more than 15,000 young people.The organisation's 2024/25 figures cover several areas of its work, including housing, education and emotional wellbeing. One measure concerns the experience of people using its services: 83% of young people surveyed said they were satisfied with the overall support Centrepoint provided.Its therapeutic services also recorded a positive response. Among young people who engaged with the charity's therapeutic services team, 93% reported that the support had made a positive difference.Education and employment preparation form another part of its work. During the year, young people receiving assistance from Skills and Employability Trainers achieved 379 certificates and qualifications. These provide a measure of progress in building skills, although the charity's work extends beyond formal learning.How Centrepoint helps young people take the next step after homelessnessMoving out of supported accommodation is an important stage for people who have experienced homelessness, but leaving a service does not automatically mean someone is prepared to live independently. Centrepoint assesses whether young people have the practical and personal readiness needed to manage that transition.For 2024/25, the charity reported that 69% of young people who left its services were ready to move into independent living. The figure offers an indication of how many had reached that stage when their support ended. It also reflects the organisation's emphasis on helping residents develop the ability to manage their next accommodation arrangements rather than simply finding them somewhere else to stay.Not every young person experiencing homelessness is already living in supported accommodation or receiving help from a housing service. Some need information about their rights, somewhere to turn for emotional support or guidance on finding suitable accommodation.Centrepoint's helpline is intended to provide that point of contact. During 2024/25, it assisted 5,166 young people, offering advice on housing rights, emotional support and access to supported accommodation. The service gives young people a way to seek help even when they are not already part of the charity's housing network.Princess Diana's connection with the charityPrincess Diana's association with homelessness charities also helped bring greater public attention to the issue. Her involvement with ‘The Passage’, another organisation working with people experiencing homelessness, became particularly significant for her family.In 1993, she took Prince William to visit The Passage for the first time. The visit introduced him to the experiences of people who relied on homelessness services and became an important part of his later involvement in the sector. The Passage has since described Diana's influence as part of the inspiration behind William's continued interest in the issue.William became Royal Patron of The Passage in February 2019. He is also Patron of Centrepoint, continuing a family connection with organisations working to support people without secure housing.Prince William's work to address homelessnessWilliam's involvement has extended beyond individual charity visits. Through Homewards, a five-year programme launched by The Royal Foundation, he has been working with organisations and communities to demonstrate how homelessness can be prevented and addressed.The Passage has a role in the initiative, contributing experience from its frontline services and helping inform longer-term approaches. The programme brings together organisations working in different areas, recognising that housing insecurity can involve a range of practical and social challenges. The royal family's association with these charities has developed over several decades, from Diana's visits to William's current patronages and public work.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2024, a Maharashtra couple lost their jobs and set off on one motorcycle with limited savings; over 80 days they rode 16,428 km across 22 states and four Union Territories, later earning record recognition
articles.summary: For Samrat and Varshali Dambe, losing their jobs in 2024 did not lead to the future they had planned.
articles.body: For Samrat and Varshali Dambe, losing their jobs in 2024 did not lead to the future they had planned. Instead, it gave them an unexpected chance to pursue a dream they had carried for years: riding a motorcycle along India’s borders.With limited savings, one motorcycle and no certainty about what awaited them after returning home, the couple from Mhapral in Maharashtra’s Ratnagiri district set out on the Art India Ride. Over 80 days, they travelled 16,428 km, crossed difficult terrain and encountered people who made unfamiliar places feel like home. Their achievement was later recognised by the India Book of Records. The journey was not planned as a record attempt. It began with a decision to stop waiting for the perfect time.A childhood sketch became a shared road tripSamrat’s idea of riding around India began when he was 12. He would draw the country’s outline and imagine following its borders on a motorcycle. Years later, the dream became something he and Varshali wanted to experience together. The couple had been riding together since 2018 and bought a Benelli TRK in 2022, hoping to take on longer journeys. Before their expedition, Samrat worked in digital marketing at a multinational company, while Varshali was a digital marketing manager at an agency.Their plans changed when both lost their jobs around June 2024. They suddenly had three to four months without the routine of work, but their finances were uncertain. “We didn’t know if we had enough money to complete the journey. We did not even know what we would do when we came back. But we knew that if we kept waiting for the right time, we might never go,” they recalled.They initially considered covering only half the country, as their savings were limited. However, by August, they had decided to begin. Heavy rain in South India also led them to change their original route just eight days before departure. They chose to start with Gujarat and travel clockwise. The couple began the Art India Ride in September 2024 and returned to Mhapral on December 8.Five bags, one motorcycle and a strict spending limitThe journey required more than enthusiasm. Their motorcycle averaged around 20 km per litre, making fuel a major expense. They set a daily budget of Rs 3,500 for fuel, food and accommodation, usually choosing rooms that cost between Rs 1,000 and Rs 1,500. They also made a practical agreement: if their savings dropped to Rs 40,000, they would return home and look for jobs.Their belongings for 80 days fitted into five bags. They carried a few clothes, riding gear, raincoats, winter layers, laptops, cameras, documents and a basic toolkit. Rather than planning every stop in advance, they generally decided where to go next a day or two before setting off. The route took them through western, northern, northeastern and southern India, including Ladakh, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Kerala and Tamil Nadu.The road did not always make things easy. Near the Gujarat-Rajasthan border, a storm and a long, isolated stretch left them anxious. In Ladakh, they faced freezing temperatures, poor network connectivity and hotels that had shut for the season. Around Pangong Lake, the temperature fell to minus 12 degrees Celsius. At Upshi, Varshali was shivering in the cold. They eventually found a local Maharashtrian who helped them arrange a room with a heater. The experience reminded them that preparation mattered, but so did knowing when to seek help.Strangers turned unfamiliar places into homeSome of the couple’s strongest memories came from people they met along the way. In Punjab, a family welcomed them into their home. In Tawang, a woman from Maharashtra offered them blessings and greeted them with a traditional Tibetan white shawl. In Bhalukpong, Arunachal Pradesh, an elderly couple running a cafe treated Samrat with the affection of a son. When the travellers returned to meet them on their way back, the uncle became emotional as they prepared to leave.Another memorable meeting happened at a breakfast stall in North Bengal. A group of people noticed the Maharashtra registration on their motorcycle and began asking about their journey. One of them, Kolkata-based corporate professional Arun Sircar, told the couple that travelling across India had once been his own dream. He and his wife later invited Samrat and Varshali home, arranged a meal and gave them a place to stay. For the couple, the meeting showed how their journey could connect with people who had never travelled the same roads. “After travelling 16,428 kilometres, it felt like one giant, compassionate family,” Samrat said, describing the warmth they received across different regions.From a record to a riding communityThe couple spent around Rs 3.75 lakh on the expedition, including fuel, food, accommodation and motorcycle maintenance. They had not set out to earn a record, but a friend encouraged them to submit their journey for recognition. They provided photographs, fuel receipts and other documents. In January 2025, the India Book of Records recognised both Samrat and Varshali as IBR Achievers for their 80-day, 16,428-km expedition. Its individual entries record the ride as covering 20 states and three Union Territories on their Benelli TRK 502X motorcycle.The experience also inspired their next step. On April 6, 2025, they started Souls of Motorcycle, a riding community intended to help enthusiasts learn, travel responsibly and build confidence on the road. According to the couple, the group has grown to more than 700 members, with over 8,000 Instagram followers. For Samrat, riding also offers a way to stay focused on the present. The sound of the engine and the attention required on the road, he says, make the experience feel like meditation.Their journey began after an unexpected career setback, with no guarantee that their savings would last. They returned with a record, new friendships and a different understanding of the country. More than the distance, the Art India Ride showed them what could happen when two people chose to begin before every uncertainty had been resolved.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A New Zealand couple bought 13 hectares of land for NZ$122,500 in 1992 and found giant old church doors; three decades later, their recycled-brick castle has towers, battlements and a secret dungeon trapdoor
articles.summary: A New Zealand couple who bought a hillside property for NZ$122,500 more than 30 years ago are now selling the unusual recycled-brick castle they spent
articles.body: A New Zealand couple who bought a hillside property for NZ$122,500 more than 30 years ago are now selling the unusual recycled-brick castle they spent three decades building and improving. Denise and Greg Powell bought the 13-hectare property at 785 Portobello Road in Broad Bay, on New Zealand's Otago Peninsula, in 1992. What began as a plan for a standard American-style house eventually became a 310-square-metre home inspired by medieval castles. It features turrets, battlements, historic building materials, and a hidden trapdoor in a hallway that leads to a basement "dungeon". The property is currently being sold by negotiation through real estate agency LJ Hooker Dunedin, according to property website OneRoof.Origins of the medieval visionThe Powells first became interested in the land after seeing it from the window of their previous home in Broad Bay. "I could look out my window and see these beautiful paddocks," Denise Powell told OneRoof. "When it came up for sale, my husband went, 'I want that.' We hadn't even walked the boundaries." The couple had already built a kit-set house and wanted something different for their new property. At first, they chose a design with two small Victorian-style turrets at either end of an American-style house. However, their plans changed after Greg Powell found two historic wooden doors, each three metres high, from a Catholic church that had been demolished in Beaumont. The couple realised that the large church doors would not fit into their original house design. They decided to change the entire plan and build the house around the rescued doors. "He led me down the garden path," Denise Powell told OneRoof, explaining how her husband slowly introduced the idea of building a castle. "If he'd said to me right up front, 'I think we should build a castle', I would have said, 'Don't be so stupid'."Architectural changes and hands-on constructionThe decision to use the huge church doors caused problems with their original draftsman. He refused to change the plans to include the historic wooden features. The couple eventually hired a recent university graduate who agreed to design a house with a castle-like layout. The construction work required plenty of physical effort from the owners. The house was built using thousands of recycled bricks. During construction, the bricks had to be lifted onto scaffolding by hand, one stage at a time. "Every night the bricklayers would leave a written sign that would say, like, 400 bricks here," Denise Powell explained to OneRoof. "At night, my dad used to go up on the scaffolding, and Greg would stand below and toss the bricks. He developed the most amazing pec muscles through that period." In the beginning, the house looked like a regular red-brick home. However, the couple added battlements along the roof in the early 2000s. This gave the building its unusual castle-like appearance.Recycled fittings and secret trapdoorThe inside of the house also includes several rescued architectural features, along with the large wooden doors from the Beaumont church. A large light fitting hanging in the centre of the main living room was salvaged from the Hermitage Hotel at Mount Cook. Greg Powell collected it using a trailer. Installing the heavy fixture required scaffolding and help from several people. One of the most unusual features is a hidden trapdoor inside a hallway cupboard. It opens into a storage space beneath the floorboards. "We used to tell the kids that came that it was the trapdoor to the dungeon, and they believed us," Denise Powell told OneRoof. "No child has ever been willing to find out." Although the couple do not have children of their own, their 13-hectare property often welcomed visiting family members. The grounds also include an outdoor tree hut and plenty of established gardens and open spaces for visitors to explore.Current market listing and future plansThe property was first put up for sale in 2024 but was temporarily taken off the market after a family tragedy. The owners have now listed the three-bedroom, three-bathroom home again as they prepare to move into a smaller property. According to OneRoof listing records, the Dunedin City Council currently gives the property a rating valuation of NZ$1.6 million. Automated market estimates place its value at around NZ$1.65 million. Listing agent Geraldine Hermens of LJ Hooker Dunedin said in the property's marketing materials that the private estate has impressive grounds. She described it as a suitable property for a family, an extended household, or a retired farmer looking for plenty of space. The Powells have already bought a smaller piece of land nearby in Broad Bay, where they plan to build their next home. "I've just turned 65 and we're future-proofing," Denise Powell told OneRoof. She explained that their next project will allow them to remain part of the coastal community where they have lived for decades.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Kodinada-Balaramapuram road widening: Contractor to be selected within a week, work by Dec
articles.summary: KRFB to pick contractor within a week for four-laning 1.6km Kodinada–Vazhimukku–Balaramapuram road; work to start by Dec after demolitions.
articles.body: Thiruvananthapuram: The long-pending four-laning of the 1.6-km Kodinada-Vazhimukku-Balaramapuram road stretch is set to move forward, with Kerala Road Fund Board (KRFB) expected to finalise the contractor within a week. Four companies have participated in the tender, and the technical evaluation is complete, while the financial evaluation is under way.KRFB officials said they would complete the financial evaluation in the coming days, after which they would select the successful bidder within a week. The agreement would be signed immediately after finalising the contractor, with the work order expected to be issued soon. The board is planning to commence construction by Dec, within a month of awarding the contract.Meanwhile, demolition of commercial establishments and shops along the stretch has begun after the completion of pending land acquisition procedures. All outstanding compensation and settlement-related cases, including rehabilitation packages for affected landowners and establishments, have reportedly been settled. The company awarded the demolition contract, has started bringing down structures from Balaramapuram Junction onwards to facilitate road widening.The project involves widening the existing stretch into a four-lane road with a proposed width of around 30.2m. The construction cost is estimated at approximately Rs 32 crore, while the overall land acquisition and compensation package is around Rs 200 crore, including compensation for land and structures.Once construction begins, the contractor will initially focus on shifting existing utilities, including electric poles and underground cables. Drainage construction will follow, after which the actual road-widening work will be taken up. The utility-shifting and drainage works are considered crucial before the existing road can be widened.The project had faced repeated delays over land acquisition and compensation disputes, with some landowners seeking enhanced compensation. The additional financial requirements and pending settlements had held up the process despite the tender being floated earlier.The road widening is expected to ease congestion along the busy Balaramapuram-Vazhimukku corridor and improve connectivity on the Karamana-Kaliyikkavila Road.Stay updated with the latest Thiruvananthapuram news. articles.title: 'NCP united under Sunetra Pawar': Party rejects rift rumours as she skips Amit Shah meet
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Nationalist Congress Party (NCP) on Monday sought to put speculation about an internal rift to rest, with party leaders dismissing reports
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Nationalist Congress Party (NCP) on Monday sought to put speculation about an internal rift to rest, with party leaders dismissing reports of differences following a high-profile meeting between Union Home Minister Amit Shah and a delegation of senior NCP leaders in New Delhi.The speculation was fuelled by the absence of Maharashtra deputy chief minister Sunetra Pawar and her sons, Parth and Jay, from Sunday's meeting with Shah. The development raised questions about whether the party's leadership was being sidelined in discussions over its future following the death of Ajit Pawar.NCP national chief spokesperson Umesh Patil rejected reports suggesting that Sunetra Pawar and Rajya Sabha MP Parth Pawar had been excluded from the Delhi discussions, describing the claims as "incorrect, baseless and misleading".Patil accused sections of the media of giving the meeting an unnecessary political angle and creating an impression that the party was divided."Attempts are being made to give an unnecessary political twist to the meeting and create a narrative of internal differences and lack of coordination within the party. The NCP is an important constituent of the Mahayuti alliance and remains united under the leadership of Sunetra Pawar," he said.He also urged the media to verify information before reporting on the party."Do not politicise formal meetings between leaders of alliance partners. Speculation should not be portrayed as fact," the NCP leader added.NCP leaders meet after Delhi parleysThe delegation that met Shah late on Sunday included Praful Patel, Sunil Tatkare, Dilip Walse Patil, Hassan Mushrif, Chhagan Bhujbal and Dhananjay Munde.After returning to Maharashtra, the leaders held closed-door discussions at Bhujbal's residence. Walse Patil, who was part of the delegation, told PTI that all the leaders who had met Shah had returned to the state."The core group will meet now and DCM Sunetra Pawar in the evening," Walse Patil said.Patil said Sunetra Pawar and Parth Pawar had met Shah earlier to discuss issues facing the party after Ajit Pawar's death. During that meeting, she had informed Shah that a delegation of senior party leaders would meet him and requested an appointment."Sunetra Pawar and Parth Pawar had earlier met Shah and discussed various issues facing the party following the death of Ajit Pawar. During that meeting, she had informed Shah that a delegation of senior party leaders would meet him and requested him to give them time," Patil said.He added that the delegation comprised senior leaders familiar with key decisions taken during Ajit Pawar's tenure, issues concerning Maharashtra and matters related to the party.The meeting with Shah comes after a setback for the NCP, which recently lost the Aurangabad Graduates constituency in the Maharashtra Legislative Council elections, a seat it had held for 18 years.It has also been seeking the finance portfolio, which was held by Ajit Pawar until his death in a plane crash in January this year.Against this backdrop, the absence of Sunetra Pawar and her sons from the Delhi meeting added to questions about coordination and decision-making within the party.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Bharathiar University Employees Union protests non-payment of Diwali advance to temporary employees
articles.summary: COIMBATORE: Bharathiar University Employees Union on Monday held a slogan-raising demonstration and a sit-in protest against the university
articles.body: COIMBATORE: Bharathiar University Employees Union on Monday held a slogan-raising demonstration and a sit-in protest against the university administration, alleging non-disbursal of Diwali festival advance to contract and temporary employees even as the festival draws near.Union general secretary M Rameshkumar said it submitted a representation to the university on Oct 13, seeking payment of a Rs 15,000 festival advance for workers ahead of Diwali. He said union representatives repeatedly pressed the registrar in person to release the amount.According to the union, the registrar had earlier said the advance would be paid after obtaining approval from the convener (higher education department secretary) on Oct 26, and that approval had also been obtained to form a committee to implement the Coimbatore collector’s minimum wage norms for the temporary employees.However, when union office-bearers met the registrar again on Oct 29, they were told that the higher education department secretary had not cleared the advance and had asked the university to seek finance committee approval, and that the issue could be reviewed after the finance committee meeting scheduled for Nov 3.The union alleged discriminatory treatment, saying a Rs 20,000 Diwali advance for permanent workers had already been approved and disbursed. articles.title: Faster mining operations to spur jobs, investment: Minister
articles.summary: Bihar mining minister Pramod Kumar urges faster clearances and time-bound e-auctions so auctioned mineral blocks start production, boosting jobs and revenue.
articles.body: Patna: Faster operationalisation of auctioned mineral blocks will help attract investment, create jobs and boost state revenue, mines and geology minister Pramod Kumar said on Monday while directing officials to expedite pending clearances and administrative procedures.Chairing a review meeting in Patna, the minister stressed faster scientific exploration, time-bound e-auctions and the early start of production and dispatch from allotted mineral blocks. “An auction is not merely a process; its real benefit will come only when production begins on time,” he said, warning that delays would not be tolerated.The meeting reviewed progress on the Pipradih-Bhurwa and Chutiya-Nauhatta glauconite blocks and the Bhora-Kathra limestone block in Rohtas district. Officials also assessed developments at the auctioned Genjana nickel-chromium and platinum group elements block in Gaya.Kumar directed officials to complete pending formalities swiftly to ensure mining projects become operational at the earliest. The minister also reviewed e-auctions of stone plots and emphasised transparent bidding and scientific surveys for the sustainable development of Bihar’s mineral resources.Department secretary Avanish Kumar, senior officials and representatives of Geological Survey of India (GSI) attended the meeting.
